paragraphs.text: A [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Menghai, made in 1996 from [sun-dried maocha](sheng:making) and pressed under high pressure into a bullet tuo. The name comes from its shape: a smaller, denser version of the [tuo](sheng:pressing), the small bowl form. Pressing began so tea could travel well, and it also sets the pace of ageing, so a format this compact and tight ages differently from a standard cake.

At thirty years it is past both the ten years some in the trade count as [aged raw pu’er](sheng:ageing) and the twenty or more that many wait for. It was made while collectors, led at first by Taiwan, were [seeking out aged raw pu’er](sheng:history-modern) through the 1990s. Like any sheng, it has changed slowly in storage rather than through a fast ferment.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
